body:
Why patronage mattered

Patronage means providing resources or support to people, institutions or activities. Buddhist monasteries required places to live, food, robes, medicines and, in many cases, land or financial support. Royal households, merchants, craft guilds and ordinary devotees contributed to these needs.

In return, Buddhist monks and nuns taught the dhamma, preserved religious knowledge and maintained communities where teaching and religious practice could continue. This relationship helped Buddhism expand beyond the areas where it first developed.

Royal patrons

Ashoka and the Mauryan period

Ashoka, the Mauryan emperor of the 3rd century BCE, was one of the most important early royal supporters of Buddhism. After the Kalinga war, he increasingly emphasised ethical conduct and non-violence. Buddhist tradition connects him with the promotion of Buddhism, pilgrimage to Buddhist sacred places and the construction or support of stupas.

Ashoka used inscriptions to communicate his policy of dhamma. His dhamma promoted moral behaviour, compassion and respect for different religious communities. Although influenced by Buddhism, Ashoka's public dhamma was not simply a command that all subjects become Buddhists.

Kanishka and the Kushanas

Kanishka, an important ruler of the Kushana dynasty around the 2nd century CE, is associated with Buddhist patronage in north-western India and Central Asia. The Kushanas controlled important parts of the Silk Roads, with major centres at Purushapura or Peshawar, Mathura and Taxila.

Buddhist tradition associates Kanishka with the holding of a Buddhist council. The poet and Buddhist scholar Ashvaghosha, who composed the Buddhacharita, is traditionally associated with his court. These associations help explain the importance of the Kushana period for Buddhist learning and cultural transmission.

Kanishka's support coincided with the growing importance of Mahayana, but he should not be described as its sole founder.

Satavahana and Pala support

Satavahana rulers were among the royal donors who contributed to Buddhist monuments in the Deccan and central India. Stupa construction and decoration often involved several different contributors rather than one king paying for an entire monument.

Much later, the Pala dynasty of eastern India, approximately the 8th–12th centuries CE, supported Buddhist monasteries and advanced learning. Nalanda and Vikramashila became important centres for students and teachers from India and other parts of Asia.

Merchants, guilds and other donors

Royal gifts were important, but Buddhism was not supported by rulers alone. Merchants could donate money, land or facilities. Guilds, which were associations of people practising a trade or craft, could contribute collectively.

At Sanchi in present-day Madhya Pradesh, donations came from kings, merchants, craft groups, monks, nuns and other devotees. A guild of ivory workers contributed to the construction of part of a stupa gateway.

In western India, Buddhist cave monasteries developed near routes crossing the Western Ghats. Sites such as Karle in present-day Maharashtra were situated near routes connecting coastal ports with inland commercial centres. Some establishments received gifts from merchants and other lay supporters, while travellers could encounter Buddhist communities along their journeys.

How donations supported the Sangha

Donations were not confined to large monuments. Monasteries required regular support. Rich merchants, landowners and kings sometimes donated land for viharas, or monasteries. Local people supplied food, clothing and medicine.

Women, men, monks and nuns could all participate in giving. The resulting support helped monastic communities remain in particular places, organise teaching and preserve Buddhist texts.

Prelims focus

  • Ashoka: Mauryan emperor of the 3rd century BCE; Buddhist patron and promoter of dhamma.
  • Kanishka: Kushana ruler associated with Buddhist patronage, a Buddhist council and Ashvaghosha.
  • Satavahanas: Among the royal donors associated with Buddhist monuments.
  • Palas: Major patrons of Buddhist monasteries and learning in eastern India.
  • Sanchi: Donations included a contribution by an ivory workers' guild.
  • Trap: Buddhist monuments were not financed exclusively by kings; merchants, guilds and other devotees also contributed.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapters 7, 8 and 10, printed pp. 71–72, 79–81 and 102–105; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, section 7.2, printed p. 96; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 3, sections on stupas and patronage, printed pp. 21 and 26; Metropolitan Museum of Art, South Asia: North, 500–1000 A.D., Key Events, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Royal, Merchant and Community Patronage of Buddhism

body:
How Buddhism travelled beyond India

Buddhism spread beyond the Indian subcontinent through the movements of monks, teachers, merchants and pilgrims. Kings and local communities sometimes supported monasteries, while travelling scholars carried texts to new places. Translation made those teachings accessible to people speaking different languages.

Its expansion followed both overland routes and maritime routes. These routes were networks with many branches rather than single roads used exclusively for religious travel.

The overland Silk Roads

From northern India, Buddhist travellers could move towards Taxila and Gandhara in the north-west. These regions were linked to Central Asia, where trade routes passed through towns and oasis settlements before reaching China.

Branches of the Silk Roads connected these regions through commercial exchanges. Merchants transported goods, while teachers and monks carried Buddhist ideas and texts. Monasteries and Buddhist shrines developed at several points along the routes.

The Kushana Empire occupied an important position in this network around the first centuries CE. Its territories connected parts of Central Asia with north-western India, and its rulers benefited from and supported activities associated with these routes.

From China, Buddhist ideas and texts subsequently spread to Korea and Japan. Chinese translations played a major role because they allowed Indian teachings to be studied without requiring every learner to know an Indian language.

Sea routes to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia

Maritime contacts connected ports of the Indian subcontinent with Sri Lanka and regions around the Bay of Bengal. Traders, monks and other travellers could continue to mainland Southeast Asia and the islands of present-day Indonesia.

Sailors used knowledge of seasonal monsoon winds to organise long-distance voyages. Commercial voyages made it possible for religious ideas and people to travel between ports and settlements.

Sri Lanka became an important centre of Theravada learning. Over subsequent centuries, Theravada became especially influential in Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. However, historical Southeast Asia also supported Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions. The Buddhist history of Indonesia, for example, cannot be described as exclusively Theravada.

Pilgrims and the movement of manuscripts

Buddhist transmission was not a one-way movement from India to other countries. Pilgrims also travelled from China to India to visit sacred places, study and obtain texts. Three Chinese Buddhist travellers are especially important:

PilgrimPeriodImportant association
Fa Xian (Faxian)Early 5th century CEVisited Buddhist centres in India and returned to China by sea, travelling through Java.
Xuan Zang (Xuanzang)7th century CETravelled overland to India, studied at Nalanda and carried Buddhist manuscripts back to China.
I-Qing (Yijing)Late 7th century CETravelled by sea and studied Buddhist learning in India and Southeast Asia.

Nalanda in present-day Bihar was an important centre of Buddhist learning visited by foreign scholars. Buddhist manuscripts obtained in India were translated into Chinese, while other translation traditions helped transmit teachings into Tibetan and additional Asian languages.

This combination of travel, study, translation and local patronage explains why Buddhism developed distinct regional forms while retaining connections with its Indian origins.

Prelims focus

  • The Silk Roads connected India, Central Asia and China through multiple overland routes.
  • The Kushanas controlled important routes linking Central Asia and north-western India.
  • Fa Xian: Early 5th-century Chinese Buddhist pilgrim who returned by sea.
  • Xuan Zang: 7th-century pilgrim associated with Nalanda and Buddhist manuscripts.
  • I-Qing: Late 7th-century pilgrim associated with maritime Buddhist travel.
  • Trap: Buddhism spread by both land and sea, and a region's Buddhist tradition could change over time.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 10, sections on the Silk Route, Buddhism and pilgrims, printed pp. 101–106; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, section How Buddhist Texts Were Prepared and Preserved, printed p. 86; UNESCO, About the Silk Roads, sections on religion and travelling the Silk Roads, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor, Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The Spread of Buddhism: Silk Roads, Sea Routes and Pilgrims

body:
Gujarat's connection with the spread of Buddhism

Gujarat formed part of the wider network of early Indian trade and religious exchange. Buddhist communities and monuments existed in different parts of the region, while royal donations and commercial contacts contributed to religious institutions.

Several Gujarat sites are important for matching a Buddhist place with its historical association. They also show that Buddhist activity in western India was not confined to one dynasty or one period.

Ashoka's rock edicts at Girnar

At Junagadh, near Mount Girnar, rock inscriptions of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka date to the 3rd century BCE. These inscriptions communicate his policy of dhamma, including ethical behaviour and respect for other religious communities.

The Girnar inscriptions connect Gujarat with Ashoka's wider imperial communication network. Their presence does not mean that Ashoka required every inhabitant of Gujarat to follow Buddhism.

Dev Ni Mori near Shamlaji

Dev Ni Mori, in present-day Aravalli district, is an important Buddhist site near Shamlaji. It is associated with a Buddhist stupa and monastery dating approximately to the 3rd–4th centuries CE.

An inscribed relic casket recovered from the stupa identifies its contents as relics of the Buddha. The site is an important example of Buddhist religious activity in Gujarat during the early centuries CE.

The Buddhist monastery at Vadnagar

Vadnagar, in present-day Mehsana district, contains remains of a Buddhist monastery dated broadly to the 2nd–7th centuries CE.

The monastery included 2 votive stupas and residential cells arranged around a courtyard. A votive stupa is a small stupa associated with a religious offering or act of devotion.

Vadnagar therefore provides another example of an organised Buddhist monastic establishment in Gujarat, distinct from the relic stupa at Dev Ni Mori.

Valabhi: Buddhist learning under the Maitrakas

Valabhi, in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, became an important centre of Buddhist learning under the Maitraka dynasty, which ruled from the late 5th to the 8th century CE.

The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Valabhi around 640 CE. The Chinese Buddhist traveller Yijing also referred to Valabhi as an important centre of Buddhist learning, alongside Nalanda.

Valabhi's Buddhist monasteries received support from Maitraka rulers. Monasteries were also founded by individuals from different social groups, including officials, merchants, religious teachers and women of prominent families.

The Maitraka example shows that the personal religious affiliation of a ruler and the institutions receiving royal support were not necessarily identical. Several Maitraka kings identified themselves as devotees of Shiva, yet their grants also supported Buddhist monasteries and communities of nuns.

Valabhi was an important Buddhist centre, but it should not be confused with Nalanda or Vikramashila, both of which were located in present-day Bihar.

Matching the major Gujarat sites

PlaceLocationMain association
GirnarJunagadhAshoka's rock edicts; 3rd century BCE
Dev Ni MoriNear Shamlaji, Aravalli districtBuddhist stupa, monastery and inscribed relic casket; 3rd–4th centuries CE
VadnagarMehsana districtBuddhist monastery with 2 votive stupas; 2nd–7th centuries CE
ValabhiSaurashtraBuddhist learning and Maitraka patronage; approximately 5th–8th centuries CE

Connecting the entire subtopic

The spread of Buddhism can be understood through 3 connected developments. First, Buddhist communities developed different spiritual traditions: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana. Second, royal and lay patronage provided monasteries and teachers with resources. Third, trade routes, pilgrimage and translation carried texts and teachings across Asia.

Gujarat's Buddhist sites belong within this wider history. Girnar reflects Mauryan communication of dhamma; Dev Ni Mori and Vadnagar show Buddhist religious establishments; and Valabhi illustrates the importance of monastic learning and patronage in early medieval western India.

Prelims focus

  • Girnar, Junagadh: Ashokan rock edicts of the 3rd century BCE.
  • Dev Ni Mori: Buddhist stupa and relic casket near Shamlaji in Aravalli district.
  • Vadnagar: Buddhist monastery in Mehsana district with 2 votive stupas.
  • Valabhi: Important Buddhist learning centre under the Maitrakas.
  • Xuanzang: Visited Valabhi in the 7th century CE.
  • Trap: Valabhi was in Gujarat; Nalanda and Vikramashila were in Bihar. Maitraka support for Buddhism does not mean every Maitraka ruler was personally Buddhist.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 4, section on early Buddhist monuments, printed p. 32; Gujarat Tourism, Ashok Edicts, Junagadh, About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Dev Ni Mori, About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Buddhist Monastery, Vadnagar, About the Place, consulted 18 November 2026; Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, Wiley, 2021, sections on Valabhi, Buddhist endowments and Chinese pilgrims, consulted 18 November 2026.]
